column3: Repeats the "thus... easy for your Lord" formula, explaining an extraordinary birth through prior creation from nothing.
Defines the effective divine speech by which a willed thing immediately comes to be.
Limits human control over the divine matter, but its judgment of repentance and punishment is not the birth decree.
Uses the same settled-decree language for an inescapable outcome, though in an eschatological setting.
Directly precedes the announcement: the messenger is sent to grant Mary a pure son.
Joins deciding a matter to "Be, and it is," directly clarifying creation without ordinary means.
Pairs a mercy from the Lord with a true, scheduled promise, but concerns a temporary barrier.
Shows the announced child speaking as God's servant and prophet, specifying the sign's later identity.
Portrays God's matter as already brought to execution, but in a battle rather than conception.
Makes restored life a sign for people and displays divine power over embodied re-creation.
States that divine willing and the command "Be" directly realize the intended object.
Relates divine will to admitting people into mercy, but not to the particular sign or birth.
Close parallel: an unmarried woman asks about a child and receives the answer of divine creative command.
Mary's immediate question about an unassisted son is the question answered in the focus ayah.
Its change of the earth's adornment to barren ground does not clarify the announced birth, sign, or decree.
Calls revelation insights, guidance, and mercy for people, closely paralleling the focus's public sign-and-mercy purpose.
Continues Jesus's self-description after birth, showing the character of the promised child.
The straightness of the revealed Book does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Combines God's arriving matter with mercy that saves, though in a destruction-and-rescue setting.
Shows that a matter settled by God cannot remain an open human option, clarifying the force of a decreed matter.
Names the messenger as mercy for all worlds, supporting the focus's description of a divinely given mercy.
Describes the Book as insights, guidance, and mercy for people, paralleling the focus's public purpose.
The immediate ensuing labor scene begins the embodied path through which the decreed birth unfolds.
Presents a divinely communicated matter as irrevocably decided, though its content is punishment.
Repeats "a mercy from Us," but in the distinct setting of temporary preservation.
Returns within the same passage to the creative-command explanation of Jesus's birth and rejects divine sonship.
Uses completion and command for the ordered heavens, only broadly analogous to the focus's decree.
Mentions mercy as a divine gift but contributes no birth, sign, or settled-matter relation.
Depicts creatures carrying out what they are commanded, supporting command's effective authority only generally.
The divinely made gardens do not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Gives Zechariah a sign involving communication with people, a nearby parallel to a miraculous birth's public sign.
Immediately supplies reassurance and water to Mary, showing mercy arriving through bodily provision.
Its rejected route and bare description of revelation do not provide positive neighbour support.
Parallels Zechariah's sign to people after a miraculous birth announcement, though with a different context.
Continues Jesus's speech by naming his blessed, worship-directed role after the announced birth.
Patience and forgiveness do not materially clarify the focus's creative decree.
Calls the Mosaic Book guidance and mercy, a remote analogue to the focus's public mercy.
A command to give open warning does not clarify the announced birth or its purpose.
The assigned functions of sun and moon do not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Explicitly joins life and death with deciding a matter and saying "Be, and it is."
Immediately directs Mary toward ripe dates, showing the practical bodily means accompanying the declared mercy.
Treats death as written and God's affair as comprehensive, but its battlefield context is remote.
Names the Quran as healing and mercy for believers, supporting mercy's beneficent function without the birth sign.
Within the same surah, recalls creation from nothing, reinforcing why the announced conception is easy for God.
Recalls first creation and a fixed meeting, but does not clarify the focus's specific mercy or birth.
Contrasts demands for a sign with signs already made clear, only broadly related to the focus's sign for people.
Argues from the greater creation of heavens and earth to human creation, supporting the ease of the miracle.
Its rejected route and instruction on communal reconciliation do not clarify the focus ayah.
Human disputation and varied parables do not materially clarify the announced birth or decree.
Immediately continues the provision with commands to eat, drink, and take comfort, completing the bodily-mercy setting.
Presents the divine command as one and instantly completed, a concise analogue to the settled matter.
Makes a destroyed people a sign for later people, clarifying public signhood while differing sharply in content.
Continues the Jesus passage with shared lordship and worship, framing the purpose of the announced child.
Places destruction at an appointed time, a distant analogue to the focus's settled decree.
Describes messengers as removing people's excuse before God, only broadly related to a sign for people.
Identifies this child as Jesus son of Mary and the true word disputed by people, directly developing the focus scene.
Moses's request for a partner in his mission does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
The brief oath about distributors of a matter offers no specific clarification of the focus.
Within the same passage, describes the matter as finally settled, extending the focus's decree language to final judgment.
Repeats "a mercy from your Lord," though as the source of a different revelatory gift.
Concludes that God's matter is to be carried out, paralleling the focus's already-effective decree in a legal narrative.
The gift of guidance and Scripture to Moses does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Forbids treating prophets as lords, supporting the servant status of Jesus developed from this birth announcement.
A human's ingratitude after receiving favor does not materially clarify the focus's birth or decree.
Shows the dispute that follows the true account of Jesus in the same passage, giving the sign's reception context.
A people's exposure to the sun does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Jacob's patience over a family matter does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Begins Mary's withdrawal from her family, supplying the narrative setting that leads directly to the focus announcement.
The divine name "the Most Merciful" shares the mercy theme but adds no specific neighbour relation.
Its instruction about wine, gambling, and spending does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
The condemned people's rejected prayer after messengers came does not clarify the focus's creative command.
A command to piety does not materially clarify the announced birth, sign, or decree.
The regret of followers in the Fire does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Continues the same passage toward the day people come before God, framing the truth of the Jesus account against later judgment.
The proposal to construct a barrier does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
A mistaken reading of restricted provision as humiliation does not materially clarify the focus.
Immediately follows the declaration with Mary's conception and withdrawal, showing the decree entering history.
A contractual term completed between Moses and Shu'ayb does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Punishment for denying signs does not materially clarify the announced sign or birth.
A command to proclaim openly does not materially clarify the focus's creative decree.
States that God grants children or makes whom He wills barren, directly supporting sovereign control of conception.
The humility of the servants of the Merciful does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
The reversal of idolaters' worship does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Uses the final settling of the matter, but only for deferred judgment.
Commands associated with miserliness do not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Knowledge of those most deserving the Fire does not materially clarify the announced birth or mercy.
States that God forms people in wombs as He wills, directly supporting divine agency in conception.
The denial of aid to the condemned does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Kind speech while awaiting mercy does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
The hypothetical human form of an angel does not materially clarify the focus's conception or decree.
A rapid extraordinary transfer displays divine favor, but lacks the focus's birth, sign, or decree structure.
A plea not to be placed with wrongdoers does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
God's watchfulness does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
The handling of public security information and mercy does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Creatures as communities and their gathering to God do not materially clarify the focus ayah.
The completion of prayer and return to work does not materially clarify the focus's settled matter.
Noah's refusal to dismiss believers does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Describes life formed and held in wombs until an appointed term, strongly illuminating the embodied course of the announced mercy.
The replacement of apostates with a beloved community does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
States that God accomplishes His matter with a measure, a general analogue to the focus's settled decree.
Directly precedes the annunciation: the Spirit appears to Mary in human form, initiating the event declared in the focus ayah.
Mary's appeal for protection records her initial response to the encounter that immediately produces the annunciation.
Mary returns carrying the child, extending the focus's decreed conception into its public, costly consequence.
The community's accusation exposes the social pressure and suffering that follow the already-settled matter.
Mary directs her people to the infant, preparing the child's speech as the public sign promised in the focus.
Jesus names his birth, death, and resurrection, extending the announced child's divinely ordered life-course.
The claim that the Most Merciful has taken a son supplies the later doctrinal error answered by the passage's account of Jesus.
Categorically rejects divine sonship, clarifying why the focus presents Jesus as a created sign and mercy rather than a divine offspring.
Names Jesus son of Mary, clear proofs, and support by the Holy Spirit, corroborating his exceptional public mission.
Rejects the claim that God has taken a son, supplying the theological premise immediately developed by 2:117's creative command.
Names Jesus son of Mary, his clear signs, and support by the Holy Spirit, directly reinforcing the announced sign's later mission.
Records Mary's election and purification, providing the immediate theological setting for the extraordinary conception.
The angels announce to Mary a son, the Messiah Jesus, as a word from God, closely paralleling the focus annunciation.
Promises that Jesus will speak to people from the cradle, directly anticipating the public sign that follows the focus.
Names the Scripture, wisdom, Torah, and Gospel that God will teach Jesus, extending the announced child's prophetic role.
Details Jesus's signs for the Children of Israel, specifying how the promised sign for people becomes publicly manifest.
Compares Jesus to Adam, created by divine command, giving a direct creation-without-ordinary-parentage analogue.
Calls Jesus the Messiah, God's messenger, and a word conveyed to Mary, while rejecting the claim that God has a son.
Recalls Jesus's speech from the cradle and his God-given signs, developing the focus's stated purpose of making him a sign.
Rejects divine sonship and affirms that God creates all things, directly supporting creation without a consort or ordinary generation.
States that Mary guarded her chastity, received the divine breath, and that she and her son were made a sign for all worlds.
Explicitly makes Jesus son of Mary and his mother a sign, and places them in a protected, provisioned setting that parallels the birth narrative.
Describes Jesus as a servant favored by God and made an example for the Children of Israel, supporting the non-divine identity developed in the passage.
States that Mary guarded her chastity and received the divine breath, a direct parallel account of the miraculous conception.
Shows Mary receiving provision from God, a close precursor to the practical provision supplied during the focus narrative.
Names Jesus son of Mary and the Gospel given to him, extending the announced child's prophetic mission.
Stresses that the Messiah and his mother ate food, reinforcing their creaturely, embodied status against divine-sonship claims.
Presents Jesus arriving with wisdom and clear exposition, continuing the public guidance role of the announced sign.
Has Jesus declare God as his Lord and theirs and call for worship, closely paralleling his declaration in 19:36.
